title: John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
summary: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness of Judea, dressed like Elijah, calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near and baptizing them in the Jordan. He warns the Pharisees and Sadducees that descent from Abraham will not save them and announces a coming one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Jesus comes to be baptized, and as he rises from the water the Spirit descends on him like a dove and the Father's voice declares him his beloved Son.
story: Nearly three decades pass between chapters 2 and 3 (Luke 3:23 says Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry). Matthew moves straight from the child in Nazareth to the adult Jesus, and he introduces him through John, the forerunner Malachi had promised. John's message of repentance and coming judgment picks up where the prophets left off, and his location, in the wilderness by the Jordan, recalls the place where Israel once crossed into the promised land. At the chapter's end Jesus passes through the waters and is declared God's Son, the same title Hosea used of Israel coming out of Egypt (2:15). The next chapter will take him, like Israel, into the wilderness to be tested.
historical:
John's ministry is also described by the Jewish historian Josephus, who calls him a good man who urged the Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another, and piety toward God, and to come together in baptism. Josephus says Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, arrested and executed John at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, because he feared his influence over the crowds. Luke dates the beginning of John's preaching to the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1), around AD 28 or 29.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were two of the main groups in the Judaism of the day. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful obedience to the law of Moses, including the traditions that applied it to daily life, and they had wide respect among ordinary people. The Sadducees were mostly from the priestly aristocracy connected with the temple; they accepted only the written law as binding and denied the resurrection of the dead. The two groups often disagreed, so it is notable that Matthew places them together under John's warning.
cultural:
Washing with water was a familiar part of Jewish life. The law required ritual washings to restore purity after contact with uncleanness, and archaeologists have found many stepped immersion pools (mikvaot) from this period in Jerusalem and elsewhere. The community whose writings were found at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, practiced repeated purifying washings. John's baptism differed in being a single act, administered by him, tied to confession of sins and preparation for the coming judgment. Some scholars think Jewish communities of the time also baptized Gentile converts, though the evidence for that practice this early is debated.

John's clothing, camel's hair with a leather belt, deliberately recalled Elijah, described in 2 Kings 1:8 as a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist. Locusts were a permitted food under the law (Leviticus 11:22), and wild honey was found in the desert; this was the food of someone living off the land. The farming images of verse 12 come from the threshing floor: harvested grain was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork so that the wind blew away the light chaff while the heavy grain fell back to be gathered, and the chaff was burned.
literary: The chapter has three scenes: John's preaching (verses 1 to 6), his warning to the religious leaders (verses 7 to 12), and Jesus' baptism (verses 13 to 17). Matthew introduces John with a fulfillment quotation from Isaiah 40:3, which in Isaiah announces God's return to lead his people home from exile. John's message in verse 2 is word for word the message Jesus will preach in 4:17, tying the two together. His speech is full of vivid images, vipers, stones, an axe, a threshing floor, and fire, all drawn from the prophets' language of judgment. The scene closes with a revelation from heaven that combines echoes of Psalm 2:7, where God addresses his anointed king as his Son, and Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his chosen servant in whom he delights and on whom he puts his Spirit.

outline.t: John preaches repentance in the wilderness
Warning to the Pharisees and Sadducees
The coming one who baptizes with the Spirit and fire
The Spirit descends and the Father speaks

doctrines.note: John calls for a change of mind and life shown in fruit, not merely in ritual or ancestry. Repentance is urgent because God's kingdom is near.

At the baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven. The church has long seen this scene as one of the clearest revelations of the one God as Father, Son, and Spirit.
The kingdom of heaven is God's reign breaking into history. John announces it as near, bringing both salvation and judgment.

John's baptism prepares for the coming one, and Jesus' own baptism becomes the pattern for the baptism he later commands (28:19). Christians differ on the mode and subjects of baptism, and nearly all traditions practice it as Jesus' command.

words.note: Metanoeo, to repent. Its Greek sense is to change one's mind, but in the Gospels it carries the weight of the Hebrew prophets' call to turn back (shuv) to God with one's whole life. John's demand for fruit in keeping with repentance shows it is not a feeling alone.

Baptizo, to dip, immerse, or wash. It was used of washing and of ritual immersion. Christians disagree on whether baptism should be by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling, and on whether it is for believers only or also for their children; the word itself is used broadly enough that each tradition appeals to it.

Dikaiosyne, righteousness. In Matthew it usually means doing what is right in God's eyes, living in line with his will (5:6, 10, 20; 6:33). Jesus' words about fulfilling all righteousness in verse 15 mean doing everything God requires, including identifying with the people he came to save.

Agapetos, beloved, and in some contexts only or unique. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Isaac, Abraham's only son whom he loved (Genesis 22:2). The Father's word, My beloved Son, speaks of Jesus' unique relationship with God.

christ: The baptism reveals who Jesus is and what he has come to do. The Father declares, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”, joining the royal Son of Psalm 2 with the servant of Isaiah 42 who will bring justice to the nations and, later in Isaiah, suffer for the sins of many. The Spirit comes upon him to equip him for his work. John rightly sees that Jesus has no sin to confess and should be baptizing him, yet Jesus insists on being baptized, standing with sinners in the water of repentance. Many interpreters see this as the first sign of his mission to take the place of his people, a mission completed at the cross, which Jesus himself later calls a baptism he must undergo (Luke 12:50). John also points forward to the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit, a promise the risen Christ fulfills at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:1-4).

hard.q: Why did Jesus, who had no sin, need to be baptized for repentance?
hard.a: John himself raises the question, and Jesus' answer is that it is fitting to fulfill all righteousness. Interpreters have understood this in several complementary ways. Some emphasize identification: Jesus stands with the people he came to save, taking his place among sinners as their representative, as the servant of Isaiah 53 is numbered with the transgressors. Others emphasize obedience: John's baptism was God's command for Israel at that moment, and Jesus submits to every part of God's will. Others see it as his public commissioning, the moment he is anointed with the Spirit and declared Son before beginning his ministry. These readings do not compete, and none implies that Jesus had sin of his own. The New Testament elsewhere states plainly that he was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15).

questions: John warns against relying on having Abraham as father. What forms of spiritual inheritance or religious background can people rely on instead of genuine repentance?
What would fruit in keeping with repentance look like in your life right now?
Before Jesus had preached a sermon or done a miracle, the Father said he was well pleased with him. What does that suggest about how God's love relates to our achievements?
